native_result.query: In what centuries did we see the highest growth phase of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE?
native_result.HypoA: Between 1500 BCE and 1300 BCE, highest growth of the period between 2000 BCE and 1100 BCE is seen.
native_result.HypoB: The highest-growth phase of the 2000-1100 BCE interval occurred in the 1400s BCE (15th century BCE). Using the study's defined growth rate, pollen_grate_100 (the percentage change of the 100-year-smoothed Belau/Woserin pollen openness score, Belau_PC1), the single peak growth rate (0.00465) falls at ~1415 BCE, and the 1400s BCE also carries the highest century-mean growth rate (+0.00193) of any century in the window. This peak is embedded in a broader, sustained upswing: the longest contiguous run of positive growth spans ~1479-1364 BCE (the 1400s BCE tailing into the 1300s BCE). This 'growth' is a local upswing in the rate of landscape opening, not net growth: the underlying smoothed openness index declines overall across the window (pollen_inter_100 falls from ~1.88 at 2000 BCE to ~1.07 at 1100 BCE). The reading is corroborated by the archaeological capital record, whose summed per-century Z-scores (capital.csv) peak sharply at 1400 BCE (Z-sum ~11.3, far above neighboring centuries).
native_result.WorkflowB: Loaded time_series_data.csv (annual, CE -4100..-500), capital.csv (century-binned, comma decimals), and the Belau/Woserin pollen openness file (comma decimals). Restricted to the 2000-1100 BCE window (CE -2000..-1100; 901 annual rows; 0 NaN in pollen_grate_100/pollen_inter_100 and all 12 capital Z-columns). Used pollen_grate_100 as the study-defined growth rate: located the single peak (max at CE -1415 / ~1415 BCE, 0.00465) and aggregated to BCE centuries (1400s BCE = highest mean +0.00193 and max 0.00465). Identified the longest contiguous positive-growth run (~1479-1364 BCE). Checked the overall pollen_inter_100 trend (net decline 1.88->1.07) to characterize growth as a local upswing. Corroborated with the capital.csv per-century Z-sum (peaks at BCE 1400, 11.28).
